title: Thiebou Guinar
localName: Thiebou guinar — thiébou guinar, riz au poulet
author: Aïssatou Mbaye
desc: The chicken thieb, with the same browned-onion colour rule and a two-onion sauce.
longDesc: Rice cooked in chicken broth with the onion-browning technique that runs through all this author's thieb recipes. Two onions for the sauce with vegetable oil, built the same way as her meat versions: the chicken browns first, the onions caramelise to a real brown, the water goes in, and the rice finishes in the broth with the liquid sitting just above the grain. She glosses the Wolof name explicitly on the page.

steps: Brown the chicken pieces in hot oil.
Add a sliced onion and diced bell pepper and keep caramelising, stirring occasionally.
Brown the onions well — they must be well browned, even brown, to get a good rice colour.
Add the water and bring to the boil.
Salt, add a fresh chilli and a bay leaf, and simmer until the chicken is cooked through.
Lift out the chicken and keep it warm.
Wash the rice and add it to the broth, with the liquid sitting slightly above the rice without drowning it.
Cover and cook until the rice is tender and the broth absorbed.
Soften the remaining onions in a little oil with a bay leaf.
When the onions turn translucent, add the chopped garlic, pepper and chilli, salt and pepper.
Add a little water and the vinegar, and cook a few minutes on low heat.
The sauce is ready when there is almost no water left.
Serve the rice with the chicken and the onion sauce.
chefTips: Same colour rule as her other thiebs and it is worth repeating: well browned, even brown, or the rice will be pale.
Chicken cooks faster than beef or lamb, so the hour that her meat versions simmer is too long here — go by the chicken.
The liquid just above the rice, never drowning it.
Vinegar in the onion sauce, as in all her versions. It is the balancing acid.
Be aware this is the thinnest-quantified of her thieb recipes: only the two onions for the sauce carry a printed amount. Nothing else has been estimated into the list above.
The sauce endpoint is almost no water left, not a number of minutes.
For a fully quantified chicken-and-rice dish from a different source, the red-palm-and-coconut version by another author is a separate tradition but better specified.
commonMistakes: Simmering chicken as long as red meat.
Too much broth with the rice.
Treating the absent quantities above as an oversight rather than as the source's own gap.
sources: Adapted from 'Thiebou Guinar — riz au poulet', aistoucuisine.com, path /publications/thiebou-guinar-riz-au-poulet. BYLINE: Aïssatou Mbaye. Date as printed: 19 décembre 2022. Yield: NONE PRINTED. TWO-PASS on every figure recovered. The page also prints 'thiébou guinar' and glosses the Wolof name explicitly.

THE PRINTED LIST, in full, is short: 'La sauce aux oignons — 2 oignons; huile végétale' with NO quantity for the oil. That is all that is quantified on the page. Every other ingredient above is NAMED in the method without an amount, and no figures have been invented. The six servings is editorial.

A SOURCING LIMIT, stated plainly: this is the thinnest-quantified of the five Mbaye thieb recipes in this collection. It is published because the chicken version is a distinct named dish in Senegalese cooking and because the author's technique cues — which are the real content of her work — are fully recorded. A reader wanting quantities should work from SEN008, which is from the same author and much better specified, and substitute chicken.

THE TECHNIQUE CUES, consistent across this author's rice dishes, as printed in French: 'Les oignons doivent être bien dorés voire brunes pour obtenir une belle couleur de riz'; 'lorsque les oignons deviennent translucides'; 'L'eau doit être un peu au dessus du riz sans le noyer'; and 'Votre sauce est prête lorsqu'il n'y a presque plus d'eau.'

A RETRIEVAL NOTE: the site is JavaScript-rendered and ingredient lists were only partially reachable. The figures recovered came from a structured data-extraction pass rather than verbatim transcription, because the retrieval layer refuses verbatim quotation beyond roughly 125 characters.

NOTE that a separate, fully quantified chicken-and-rice dish by a different author — Senegalese chicken thighs with red palm and coconut rice — exists in the researched material and is a different dish rather than a variant of this one.
reheating: Steam the rice; warm the chicken gently.
healthBenefits: No bouillon in the author's method, so lower in sodium than most published versions.
Onions supply quercetin, concentrated by long browning.
culturalNote: Guinar is chicken in Wolof, and thiebou guinar is the Sunday version of the weekday meat thieb — cheaper than fish, quicker than lamb, and built on the same hour of patient onion-browning that every good thieb depends on.
